what_it_does: WebAssembly (Wasm) is a compact code format used to run untrusted programs safely inside web browsers and cloud services; to prevent a rogue program from reading or corrupting memory it shouldn't touch, the runtime wraps it in a 'sandbox' using a technique called Software-based Fault Isolation (SFI), which inserts extra checking instructions before every memory access. Those extra checks add measurable slowdown, and fitting many sandboxed programs into a single process is limited because each sandbox needs its own reserved slice of the address space (the numerical range of memory a process can see). Segue exploits a rarely-used feature of x86-64 processors — segment registers called FS and GS — to encode the legal memory boundary of each sandbox directly in hardware, so the processor enforces the limit automatically without any extra check instructions; this alone removes nearly half of Wasm's overhead on one benchmark set. ColorGuard then uses memory protection keys (a hardware feature that 'colors' ranges of memory with a tag, similar to painting rooms different colors so a visitor with the wrong key is automatically blocked) to give each Wasm instance its own color, allowing up to 15 times more concurrent sandboxed programs to coexist in the same process.
